name: Apartheid
summary: Apartheid was the National Party's doctrine of racial separation in South Africa, 1948-1990s, under which every person was classified by race, political power stayed with the white minority and the other groups were assigned separate institutions and homelands. It justified this as Christian guardianship and the right of each people to its own development, and it met opposition with a security state and bans on communism and on the ANC. It was a statist, Afrikaner-nationalist and anti-communist regime.
scope: The official ideology and record of the National Party governments of 1948-1990 (Malan, Strijdom, Verwoerd, Vorster, Botha): its statutes and the stated policy of its prime ministers, with the TRC's findings on how the state behaved. It is one regime doctrine, not a family of movements; its ideology is answered from its own statutes, speeches and record, and Afrikaner nationalism as such, South African liberalism and the post-1990 reforms are left out.

missingStatements.text: Voting rights should be limited to members of one racial group.
missingStatements.rationale: The state confined the national vote to whites, struck Coloured voters from the common roll in 1951 and gave Africans no national vote.

missingStatements.text: Each ethnic group should have its own homeland with its own government, apart from the others.
missingStatements.rationale: The Promotion of Bantu Self-government Act of 1959 and later laws created ethnic homelands, four of them nominally independent, which Verwoerd presented as the answer to a multiracial state.

missingStatements.text: Communist doctrine and organisations should be outlawed.
missingStatements.rationale: The Suppression of Communism Act banned the Communist Party in 1950 and let the minister ban any body or person held to promote communism.

notes: Answers rest on the apartheid statutes (read in full text) and the stated policy and record of its governments. Silence is null, including the Marxist-doctrine statements the regime banned without rebutting, the moral and family questions, and most economic ones. Late reforms under P.W. Botha (the 1983 constitution, the 1985 repeal of the mixed-marriage ban, the 1986 end of pass laws) changed the form but not the core of the system and don't change the mature answers. Several answers (state presidency, courts, parastatals) rest on the regime's constitutional and economic record rather than on apartheid doctrine proper.
